summary: The machine has the needed data-plane MCP server, Microsoft Learn access, Python, and the DocumentDB agent skills required to build the Beanie + LangChain orchestrator. The build can start, but several cold answers were incorrect or ambiguous (resource types, CLI groups, billing model, connection-string host/ports, local dev image/port, vector & text index creation APIs, service name history). The builder should follow the installed documentdb-* skills and the Microsoft Learn pages cited below and add a few small developer conveniences (mongosh or clear instructions to use the MCP server instead).
summary_points: All required runtime pieces to write and verify the sample are present: python (3.13), pip, documentdb MCP server, Microsoft Learn search server, and the documentdb-* skills.

Several cold answers were wrong or mixed up with Azure Cosmos DB (RU) or Amazon DocumentDB — key mistakes include the resource type (mongoClusters vs databaseAccounts), CLI command group (az documentdb mongocluster...), and billing model (vCores/tiered vs RU/s).

Vector and full-text search are native features with distinct creation APIs (cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions and createSearchIndexes/$search); the cold answers that recommended external Azure Cognitive Search or generic createIndex calls were inaccurate.
Local development should use the DocumentDB Gateway container (port 10260), not a generic Mongo docker image on 27017 — local gateway guidance is in the installed documentdb-local-deployment skill.

No blocking missing tools — the build can proceed — but add mongosh (or instruct agents to use the documentdb MCP server) and resolve small doc/assumption gaps (LLM/provider, pinned deps, sample data schema).

tools.name: python
tools.needed_for: Run the sample app, install project dependencies, run seed and orchestrator scripts (Beanie + LangChain).
tools.detail: Python 3.13.13 (python resolves to virtualenv as described in skill_md).
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run or test the sample locally.
tools.workaround: Install Python 3.11+ and use virtualenv; the repo should include a requirements.txt and .env.example.

tools.name: pip
tools.needed_for: Install Python dependencies (Beanie, motor, pymongo, langchain, etc.).
tools.workaround: Use pip bundled with python, or use pipx/poetry if preferred; document process in README.

tools.name: documentdb MCP server (connection_profile: default)
tools.needed_for: Data-plane verification: list databases, create collections/indexes, run queries, explain plans, sample documents inspection and the findAndModify atomic update verification.
tools.detail: documentdb MCP server present in inventory with 18 data-plane tools (list_databases, create_index, find_and_modify, explain, aggregate, etc.).
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder couldn't inspect or verify what the sample created on the live cluster without direct mongosh access; tests that call data-plane would be harder to validate.
tools.workaround: Use direct Python driver calls to inspect DB if MCP server absent; but MCP simplifies validations. All MCP operations must specify connection_profile "default".

tools.name: Microsoft Learn MCP server (learn_microsoft_docs_search / learn_microsoft_docs_fetch)
tools.needed_for: Authoritative grounding of API shape, CLI commands, index creation syntax, vector-search and full-text search docs used to resolve cold-answer confusions.
tools.detail: learn MCP tools available in inventory.
tools.impact_if_missing: No quick, machine-queryable access to Microsoft Learn pages; increased risk of using stale or incorrect assumptions.
tools.workaround: Manually collect canonical docs and include them in repo; rely on installed documentdb-* skills (which embed references).

tools.name: az (Azure CLI)
tools.needed_for: Inspect cluster control-plane details (provider registration, resource type checks, retrieving connection strings if necessary, enabling preview features such as FullTextSearch or Change Streams).
tools.detail: Azure CLI available (2.89.1) and signed-in (az login present).
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to inspect cluster-level configuration and enable features (but not required to run the sample against an already-provisioned cluster).
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP server and/or portal to inspect cluster properties; ask an admin to enable features.

tools.needed_for: Optional: manual interactive DB inspection and quick commands (create indexes, inspect documents) outside MCP server tooling.

tools.workaround: Use documentdb MCP server tools (documentdb_find_documents, documentdb_list_indexes, documentdb_create_index, documentdb_find_and_modify) for all verifications; or install mongosh locally.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft.DocumentDB (resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts).
confusions.grounded_answer: Resource provider: Microsoft.DocumentDB; resource type for this managed MongoDB service is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Same provider namespace (Microsoft.DocumentDB) and historical overlap of names: older Cosmos DB resources (databaseAccounts) used similar names; the cold answer describes the Cosmos DB account resource (databaseAccounts) rather than the dedicated DocumentDB mongoClusters resource.

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb create (Cosmos DB accounts docs)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder used databaseAccounts in ARM/Bicep/Terraform or tried az cosmosdb commands, they would attempt to manage the wrong resource type and fail to create/manage the DocumentDB cluster (or configure wrong APIs).
improvements: Update the top-level quickstart and any agent skill descriptions to explicitly state 'resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters' when referring to this managed MongoDB product (documentdb-azure-deployment).
Add a deprecation/clarification sentence on the older 'databaseAccounts' pages warning readers not to confuse Cosmos DB account types with the new mongoClusters resource.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group (core CLI). Example to create: az cosmosdb create -g MyRG -n my-docdb-account --kind MongoDB
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the az documentdb mongocluster command group (az documentdb mongocluster create / az documentdb mongocluster show / az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings). The az documentdb command group is available in the Azure CLI (documentdb commands are part of the CLI command surface).

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used 'az cosmosdb' which manages Cosmos DB databaseAccounts; the new dedicated DocumentDB cluster resource has its own az documentdb command group (mongocluster) and different parameters.
confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb commands would try to create a Cosmos DB account (RU-based) not the vCore-based DocumentDB cluster, causing the wrong resource to be provisioned or CLI errors.
improvements: Add an explicit example in the CLI quickstart pages showing 'az documentdb mongocluster create' and a short note 'do not use az cosmosdb for Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters' so agents and humans do not conflate the two CLI groups.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform (azurerm provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account.
confusions.grounded_answer: Bicep/ARM resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters. Terraform: azurerm_mongo_cluster (or use AzAPI targeting Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters).

grounding_links.title: Terraform azurerm_mongo_cluster (reference via AzureRM provider docs)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described the ARM/Terraform resource types for Cosmos DB accounts (databaseAccounts / azurerm_cosmosdb_account) rather than the dedicated mongoClusters resource and the Terraform azurerm_mongo_cluster resource introduced for vCore clusters.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong ARM/Terraform resource would produce a Cosmos DB account (different billing and behavior) or an IaC plan that fails when trying to target mongoClusters with the wrong resource type.
improvements: Document the Terraform resource 'azurerm_mongo_cluster' and include a Bicep snippet that targets Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters in the agent kit templates so generated IaC is correct by default.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: A typical connection string follows the MongoDB URI form: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account-name>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false  (TLS on port 10255, ssl=true, replicaSet=globaldb, retryWrites often set to false for Cosmos Mongo API).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB cluster connection strings use MongoDB URI/SRV forms but with the DocumentDB cluster host and options. Example (from docs): mongodb+srv://<user>:<password>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retrywrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000. (Host suffix and port differ from old Cosmos DB Mongo API examples like .mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255.)
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used the connection-string shape and host suffix typical of the older Cosmos DB 'MongoDB API' (account-name.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255). The managed DocumentDB mongoClusters use a different host suffix (e.g., .global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com) and recommended options (tls=true, authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC or SCRAM-SHA-256 depending on auth).
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used the wrong host suffix or port, connections would fail (DNS mismatch) or drivers would try unsupported options (wrong auth mechanism).
improvements: Clarify connection-string examples in agent-kit README: show both SRV (mongodb+srv) and standard URIs for DocumentDB clusters and explicitly show the cluster host suffix (.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com) and recommended options.
Add a short code snippet in documentdb-connection skill that extracts the right options from DOCUMENTDB_URI and demonstrates driver-specific tuning (maxPoolSize, tls, retryWrites=false).

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Capacity is billed as Azure Cosmos DB throughput (Request Units / RU/s) or serverless where supported. (Provisioned RU/s is the primary billing model for Cosmos DB Mongo-compatible accounts.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (the managed MongoDB/vCore product) is billed by compute tier (vCore-style tiers: M10, M20, M30, ...), storage, and optional features; it is not billed as RU/s. The service's docs and the documentdb-azure-deployment skill explicitly use compute tier names (M10..M200).

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB at a glance (pricing and tiers)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described Cosmos DB's RU model (which applies to Cosmos DB for NoSQL and Cosmos Mongo API RU-mode) instead of the dedicated vCore/compute-tier model used by the DocumentDB mongoClusters product.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB RU model docs

confusions.build_risk: Using RU-based commands or assumptions (e.g., expecting RU/s autoscale or provisioning RU throughput) would lead to incorrect capacity planning and incorrect IaC templates for this service.
improvements: Add a short 'Billing & capacity' snippet to the documentdb-azure-deployment quickstart that contrasts vCore/tiered billing (Mxx) with Cosmos RU-based billing and warns readers not to mix the two.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary auth is Mongo-style credentials (username/password / SCRAM). Some Cosmos DB-ish deployments support Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) token-based auth for the Mongo API; in that case the app obtains an AAD access token (via azure.identity) and supplies it to the driver per the provider's OAUTH/SASL flow.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports native (SCRAM) authentication and Microsoft Entra ID (token-based / OIDC) authentication. To use Entra ID, enable MicrosoftEntraID in the cluster's authConfig, then clients supply an Entra-issued OIDC access token and use authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC (or the driver OIDC flow). The Microsoft Learn how-to describes enabling Entra ID and the OIDC connection examples.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a — the cold answer described the general mechanism; Microsoft Learn provides the precise 'MONGODB-OIDC' examples and the need to enable MicrosoftEntraID on the cluster.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumed Entra ID was enabled by default they might fail to connect; the cluster must be configured to allow MicrosoftEntraID.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers (e.g., pymongo or motor for Python). There isn't a different Mongo-specific SDK for the Mongo-compatible endpoint; use MongoDB's driver for your language.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo / motor / MongoClient / motor_asyncio). For Python with Beanie, use motor.motor_asyncio.AsyncIOMotorClient and init_beanie with your document models. There is no separate service-specific Mongo SDK for application CRUD; the drivers work with the DocumentDB wire protocol.
confusions.build_risk: Low — follow the documentdb-driver guidance for singleton clients and connection pooling.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Vector/indexing support varies; commonly supported algorithms in cloud Mongo-compatible offerings include HNSW, IVF and DiskANN. Creation typically uses a collection-level index API rather than a simple Mongo createIndex; a representative (non-guaranteed) example: db.runCommand({ createIndexes: 'loan_applications', indexes: [ { key: { embedding: 'knn' }, name: 'embedding_knn', algorithm: 'hnsw', dims: 1536 } ] });

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector-search)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer guessed supported algorithms correctly but gave a generic or inaccurate createIndex payload (using key: { embedding: 'knn' } and algorithm fields) that doesn't match DocumentDB's 'cosmosSearchOptions' JSON shape.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder tried to create a vector index with the wrong JSON shape the API call would fail; vector queries would not be possible until the index is created with the correct options (kind, dimensions, algorithm-specific args).
improvements: Add the exact createIndexes/cosmosSearchOptions JSON examples to the documentdb-vector-search skill and include one Python+PyMongo example showing the db.command(...) body to create HNSW/IVF/DiskANN indexes.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Full-text is typically provided by an integrated search engine or by integrating with Azure Cognitive Search. Hybrid (vector + text) search is done by combining the vector index (KNN) with text scoring from the search engine (e.g., Azure Cognitive Search or a provider-specific search index) and merging results in the application.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides built-in full-text search (BM25) via createSearchIndexes + $search (BM25) and built-in vector search (cosmosSearch). Hybrid retrieval (BM25 + vector) is supported server-side by combining the two indexes in one aggregation pipeline, e.g., via server-side Reciprocal Rank Fusion or $unionWith. You do NOT need an external Azure Cognitive Search for in-cluster hybrid search.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn (full-text and hybrid search pages)

grounding_links.title: Hybrid search (BM25 + vector) in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed external search integration (Azure Cognitive Search) common in some architectures; DocumentDB embeds BM25-style full-text search and supports server-side fusion with vector search.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cognitive Search usage patterns (external to database)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder wired the sample to an external search service they would add unnecessary complexity and a separate index pipeline; the sample should use built-in createSearchIndexes and $search with cosmosSearch if hybrid retrieval is desired.
improvements: Add a short example in the documentdb-full-text-search skill showing a combined aggregation pipeline that runs $search (BM25) and cosmosSearch (vector) and fuses results server-side with $unionWith or RRF.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Expect MongoDB wire protocol compatibility advertised by the service (many offer 4.x/5.x/7.0-level compatibility depending on SKU). Some Cosmos/Mongo-compatible services lag behind official MongoDB server feature parity: server-side JS ($where), certain aggregation pipeline stages, or some storage-engine-specific features may be missing or behave differently. Verify the cluster's advertised MongoDB wire version before relying on cutting-edge server features.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 (and documents provide exact operator/stage compatibility). Some admin commands are not exposed; check the 'MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility' reference for exact operator/stage coverage. The service advertises ~99.03% operator compatibility and documents the exceptions.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (wire protocol versions)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer was vague and conservative; the service actually documents explicit supported wire protocol versions and percentage operator compatibility.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumed only older protocol versions were supported they might avoid newer driver features unnecessarily or target an older API surface.
improvements: Add an explicit 'Supported wire protocol versions' line to the agent kit README (5.0–8.0) and link to the MQL compatibility matrix so builders don't guess.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: For MongoDB-compatible development run the official MongoDB docker image (e.g., mongo:7.0) on port 27017. The Azure Cosmos DB Emulator exists but historically does not fully support the MongoDB API; prefer a local Mongo image for driver-level development.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the DocumentDB Gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) which exposes the MongoDB protocol on port 10260 and supports TLS and SCRAM-SHA-256. The documentdb-local-deployment skill explains port 10260, TLS settings and env-driven seed options.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer recommended the generic official MongoDB image (common for many Mongo-compatible stacks) but DocumentDB provides a specific local Gateway image with cluster-like behavior and a nonstandard port (10260).
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used a vanilla mongo:7.0 image they would miss DocumentDB features (vector search, built-in full-text search, the same auth configs and gateway behaviors) and tests might not be representative. The sample should use the DocumentDB local gateway if local parity is required.
improvements: Incorporate the local Gateway image + minimal docker-compose snippet into the sample repo README (documentdb-local-deployment skill already contains the canonical guidance).

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Many Mongo-compatible services expose change streams if they support the MongoDB wire protocol version that includes them; where not available you must use the provider's change feed (Cosmos DB change feed). If supported, change streams usually work out of the box but may require specific account tiers or a replica/clustered setup.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports change streams. For multishard clusters or certain scenarios you may need to enable a preview feature for multishard change streams; the docs describe enabling change streams in cluster Features and show example usage (Model.watch()/db.collection.watch()).
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn (change-streams docs + Azure Functions docs)

grounding_links.title: Azure Functions trigger for DocumentDB (uses change streams)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes change streams are always enabled by default on multishard clusters they might miss the required preview/feature toggle; verify cluster features before tests.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb MCP server (service-specific) for data-plane inspection and tools; the general Azure MCP server covers control-plane operations but the documentdb MCP server provides the specialized data-plane capabilities for this service.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the documentdb MCP server supplies data-plane tools (list_databases, create_index, find_and_modify, explain, etc.). The general Azure MCP server is for control-plane and higher-level guidance.
confusions.grounding_source: machine inventory (documentdb MCP server tools list)

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Microsoft used the name Azure DocumentDB for the original JSON-document DB service that later became Azure Cosmos DB. 'Azure DocumentDB' as a name predates Cosmos DB; the Cosmos platform now includes multiple APIs (SQL, MongoDB-compatible, etc.). This is distinct from any third-party/open-source project named DocumentDB; don't confuse with AWS DocumentDB or other similarly named projects.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly true but ambiguous: the current managed MongoDB offering was formerly named 'vCore-based Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB' and has been renamed to 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)'. This service is distinct from the original 'Azure DocumentDB' product that became Cosmos DB many years ago; it is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (governed by the Linux Foundation) and not related to Amazon DocumentDB.

grounding_links.title: How does Azure DocumentDB relate to Azure Cosmos DB? (FAQ)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Multiple historical renames and the reuse of the 'DocumentDB' name across different Microsoft products make the lineage confusing; the cold answer mixed the original 2014 DocumentDB → Cosmos story with the newer rebranding of vCore-based Cosmos Mongo to 'Azure DocumentDB'.

confusion_sources.title: Old blog posts and docs that still use 'vCore' or 'Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' names

confusions.build_risk: Naming confusion could lead builders to follow older Cosmos DB quickstarts or use the wrong CLI/ARM resource types.
improvements: Add a short 'Naming & history' banner in the agent kit READMEs clarifying 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) — formerly vCore-based Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB — is different from the original Azure DocumentDB that became Cosmos DB in 2017; also not Amazon DocumentDB.'

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: The underlying engine is the provider's (Azure Cosmos DB) proprietary engine exposing a MongoDB-compatible wire protocol. Application code should use standard MongoDB drivers, but expect small differences in supported features, behavior, and performance characteristics (some server-side features or admin commands may be absent or behave differently).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (the DocumentDB project) and is not the Cosmos DB proprietary engine; it is exposed via the MongoDB wire protocol. Application code uses standard MongoDB drivers, but the underlying engine is DocumentDB (open-source), which provides some operational differences and additional features (integrated vector search, etc.).

grounding_links.title: What is DocumentDB (in Azure) — implementation note

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer assumed a proprietary Cosmos engine; the product is actually built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (the two are related historically but distinct), which is important for portability and licensing claims.

confusion_sources.title: Generic marketing pages that refer to Cosmos DB engine

confusions.build_risk: Minor for writing the sample (drivers remain the same), but mistaken licensing/portability assumptions (e.g., 'can't run engine elsewhere') could lead to wrong guidance in README or migration notes.
improvements: State clearly in the repo README and agent docs that the service is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine, and include the GitHub reference link so builders understand portability and license implications.

confusions.question: What database name should the sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the database sample_fintech_14 for everything the sample creates and queries.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the run-environment (sample prompt skill_md) specifies 'use database sample_fintech_14' for this sample.

confusions.question: How does the sample connect to the cluster at runtime?
confusions.cold_answer: Read the full MongoDB connection URI from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it directly to the MongoDB driver (e.g., pymongo.MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']) or motor.motor_asyncio.AsyncIOMotorClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI'])).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the run-environment instructs the sample to read DOCUMENTDB_URI from the environment at runtime and use it for driver connections (use TLS and recommended driver options).

confusions.question: Which Python ODM setup will the sample use with Beanie?
confusions.cold_answer: Use motor.motor_asyncio.AsyncIOMotorClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI'], tls=True) to get the database object, then call await init_beanie(database=db['sample_fintech_14'], document_models=[LoanApplication, TransitionLog]).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct and consistent with documentdb-driver guidance: use an AsyncIOMotorClient singleton, pass the db to init_beanie with the document models, and ensure driver options include TLS and any recommended DocumentDB tuning (e.g., retryWrites=false).
confusions.build_risk: If the builder created multiple clients per request the sample could see connection pool exhaustion; follow the singleton pattern.

confusions.question: How will the orchestrator perform an atomic state transition and log the transition in one operation?
confusions.cold_answer: Use a single find_one_and_update (optimistic concurrency) that filters on the current state and updates state + appends a transition log entry, e.g. pymongo: result = collection.find_one_and_update({'_id': id, 'state': expected_state}, {'$set': {'state': new_state}, '$push': {'transitions': transition_obj}}, return_document=ReturnDocument.AFTER). If transactions are available on the cluster, run these in a session transaction.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use findOneAndUpdate / find_one_and_update with a filter on expected current state and $push the transition in the same update for atomicity; if multi-document atomicity is required use a transaction (if supported) via sessions. documentdb_find_and_modify and documentdb_find_and_modify MCP tool mirror this pattern.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb MCP server tools + documentdb-driver skill
confusions.build_risk: If the builder tries an unconditional update without filtering on the expected current state they risk lost updates/ races.

confusions.question: What indexes will the sample create to make the orchestrator efficient?
confusions.cold_answer: Create at least: an index on state (db.loan_applications.create_index([('state',1)])), an index on applicationId/_id (default), and a descending created_at index (('created_at', -1)). If vector search is used, create the provider-specific vector index on the embedding field via the cluster's vector-index API (example: a KNN/HNSW index named embedding_knn for the embedding field).
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly correct: the basic sample should create an index on current_state and created_at; if vector search is used the sample must create a cosmosSearch vector index (vector-ivf/vector-hnsw/vector-diskann) via createIndexes with cosmosSearchOptions. For standard orchestrator flows these simple scalar indexes are sufficient; vector/index creation uses the provider-specific JSON shapes documented in the vector-search docs.

grounding_links.title: Vector search docs (create vector index example)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer mixed generic index advice (which is correct for current_state) with a generic vector-index example; the vector index must use cosmosSearchOptions shape rather than a generic 'knn' key.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder attempts to create a vector index using a generic create_index call that doesn't include the provider-specific options the call will fail; create the vector index using the documented cosmosSearchOptions payload.
improvements: Add an example 'create state index' and a separate 'create vector index' (cosmosSearchOptions JSON) to the sample repo so builders don't conflate the two.

information_gaps.title: LLM provider and model choice
information_gaps.description: The prompt asks for LangChain 'specialist agents' but does not specify which LLM provider or model (OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, local stub). None of the DocumentDB skills or Microsoft Learn pages dictate this choice. The builder must be told whether to include real LLM calls (requiring API keys) or to stub agents for a reproducible demo.

information_gaps.title: Pinned dependency versions
information_gaps.description: No single authoritative source in the skills or docs specifies exact recommended versions of Beanie, motor, pymongo, or LangChain to use together on this machine (Python 3.13). The documentdb-driver skill gives patterns but not a pinned requirements.txt. The builder needs to decide pinned versions and test them.

information_gaps.title: Sample data schema choices and field names
information_gaps.description: Prompt suggests a state-machine document but does not mandate concrete field names or types (e.g., 'current_state' vs 'state', transition-log shape). The agent skills provide modeling guidance but not a single canonical schema the sample must use.

information_gaps.title: Do we require live LLM calls in the end-to-end verification?
information_gaps.description: No doc or skill mandates whether the runnable example must perform real external LLM calls for underwriting/compliance decisions. If API keys are absent, builder must choose deterministic stub agents; the sample README should state the chosen approach.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters as the ARM/Bicep/Terraform resource type (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts); create clusters with az documentdb mongocluster create or the provided Bicep template.

Read the connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI and use the cluster host suffix and options shown in the service docs (mongodb+srv://<user>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retrywrites=false). Do not assume the old .mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255 form.

sources.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

guidance_for_builder.instruction: For atomic state transitions use a single findOneAndUpdate / find_one_and_update that filters on the expected current state and $pushes the transition record in the same update; use driver sessions / transactions only if you require multi-document atomicity and the cluster tier supports it.

If you need local dev parity, run the DocumentDB Gateway container (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) and connect on port 10260 with TLS and SCRAM-SHA-256, following documentdb-local-deployment guidance.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample: the run-environment provides a live cluster and az is present. If the team wants to include an 'azd' deployment path, instruct how to install azd in the repo or CI. For now, omit azd-based deployment paths.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Bicep is not required to build or run the sample (the cluster already exists). If you want to include IaC Bicep samples for completeness, provide the Bicep template in the repo or document how to install the bicep CLI (`az bicep install`).

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required to build the sample. If the repo wants to ship Terraform IaC examples, include them in examples/ with instructions to install Terraform. Otherwise rely on the provided cluster.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not necessary for this Python+Beanie sample. Add only if you plan to add .NET examples.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh for local, interactive troubleshooting and quick manual checks (install via npm: `npm install -g mongosh` or from MongoDB downloads). Alternatively instruct that the documentdb MCP server tools are the supported verification interface for agents.
